hookLine: On the drawing, it looks like the same thing.

captions.text: Kansas City, Missouri. January 1979.

In a fabricator's shop, somebody redraws one
detail on a hotel walkway.

One long steel rod becomes two shorter ones, four
inches apart.
Nobody has ever established whose hand drew it.

Two walkways will hang from that detail,
over a crowded room.
On the drawing, it looks like the same thing.

That detail is a nut, a washer, and a hole
through a steel beam.

It does not get weaker when the second rod
arrives.
It is simply asked to carry twice as much.

The Hyatt Regency Hotel in Kansas City
had been open about a year.
At its centre was an atrium.

A room roughly a hundred and seventeen feet
by a hundred and forty-five,
and fifty feet high.

Three suspended walkways spanned it,
at the second, third and fourth floor levels.

They were bridges with nothing underneath them.
No columns, no piers, no arch.

Steel rods coming down out of the roof,
and the walkway hanging on the rods.

So the whole question in this building,
from the day it was drawn, is a small one.
What holds the rod. Two of the three were stacked.

The second floor walkway was suspended
from the fourth floor walkway,
which was directly above it.
The third was offset from the other two,

and hung on its own rods from the roof framing.
Remember that one.

It is the reason the third walkway is still
standing at the end of this film.
Each walkway was four spans of steel stringers.
Underneath the stringers ran a pair of box beams,

and the box beams were what the rods actually
held.
A box beam sounds like a solid thing. It was not.
It was two ordinary eight-inch steel channels,

laid facing each other and joined toe to toe
by continuous longitudinal welds.
A hollow rectangle, closed along two seams.
The rods were an inch and a quarter across,

threaded top and bottom to take a nut
and a washer. That is the whole connection.

A rod through a hole. A washer under the beam.
A nut under the washer.

There is nothing else in it. As it was first
drawn, one rod ran the whole way down.

Out of the roof framing, through the fourth floor
box beam,
and on down through the second.
Each beam sat on its own nut, on the same rod,

and each beam put only its own share
into the steel.

The Missouri Court of Appeals calls it, plainly,
a one rod design. Six rods.

Three down each side of the atrium. Thirty feet
of threaded steel apiece.

Now the arithmetic, because this film
is arithmetic.

The project specified a design live load
of a hundred pounds per square foot
for hotel corridors and lobby areas,

and the federal investigators read
that as covering the walkways.

Engineers write that load in kips. A kip
is a thousand pounds of force.

It is not a mysterious unit. It is a weight,
written short.

Under the one rod design, the load arriving
at each connection,
at the second floor and at the fourth,
would have been about twenty point three kips.

The same at both levels, because each beam carried
only itself.

Steel design in Kansas City ran on the AISC
Specification.

That is what the city's building code pointed
at for structural steel.

Under that specification a connection carries
a factor of safety.

The lowest that would govern any part of this one
is one point six seven.
Multiply the design load by that,

and you have the load the finished connection
is expected to survive

before it lets go. For the one rod design,
that is thirty-three point nine kips.

The connection as drawn could take about twenty
point five.
Sixty percent of what the code expected.
That percentage is the federal report's own.

So the detail was already illegal before anybody
changed it.

The Missouri Board's tribunal found
that the hanger rods and the connections shown

on the structural drawings did not meet the design
specifications

of the Kansas City Building Code, and that finding
was not contested on appeal.

The federal report reached it separately,
from the steel.

There is one more thing about that drawing, and it
is not a small one.

The connection had no calculations behind it
that anybody has ever seen.

Not the federal investigators. Not the Office
of the Mayor.

Efforts to obtain copies of the structural design
calculations, the report says,

were unsuccessful. A tribunal would later find
that these were special connections,

and that all connections are the responsibility
of the structural engineer.

And it found something harder than special. It
found them non-redundant.

A non-redundant connection which fails will cause
collapse of the structure.

Six of them, over a room that held two thousand
people.
Nothing behind any of them if one let go.

Construction was under way while the design
was still being finished.
The Hyatt was a fast-track project,

which means the building went
up while the drawings were still being drawn.
The steel fabricator was Havens Steel Company.

Havens had engineers of its own, capable
of designing simple, complex,
or special connections.
Because of certain fabricating problems,

Havens proposed a double rod system to the project
engineer.

Two explanations have been proposed
in the literature for why.
One is that rods long enough could not be got.

The other is that threading a thirty-foot rod
along its whole length was judged
impractical. Both are proposals.

Neither is a finding of any tribunal,
and this film does not choose between them.
Here is what the change did.

Instead of one rod carrying two beams at two
different heights,
there were now two rods.

An upper set from the fourth floor box beams
to the roof framing.

A lower set from the second floor box beams
up to the fourth.
The second rod did not pass through the same hole.

It was offset four inches along the beam. Follow
the load.
Under the new arrangement,

all of the second floor walkway load was first
transferred
to the fourth floor box beams.

Then that load, and the fourth floor walkway's own
load,

both went out through the fourth floor connections
into the ceiling rods.
The second floor connection did not change at all.
It still carried about twenty point three kips.

The fourth floor connection went to about forty
point seven.

The word the federal report uses is doubled,
and it uses it as a conclusion.

The change in hanger rod arrangement,
from a continuous rod to interrupted rods,

essentially doubled the load to be transferred
by the fourth floor connections.

The Missouri Court of Appeals says the same thing,
in its own words,
out of its own record.

The effect of this change was to double the load
on the fourth floor walkway

and on the connections there. No steel
was removed. No steel was thinned.
One beam was simply asked to carry two.

The change was transmitted to the project
engineer, and it was approved.
There was evidence, the court found,

that one of the architects contacted the project
engineer to verify

that the double rod arrangement was structurally
sound, and was advised that it was.
On appeal the engineers disputed that.

The court reviewed the record and rejected
the dispute.

It is a reasonable inference from the evidence,
the same court wrote,

that the engineering calculations and tests
necessary

to determine whether the double rod design
was sound were never made.
Somebody did notice.

A technician checking the shop drawings called
the project engineer's attention
to questions about the strength of the rods,
and about the change from one rod to two.

He was told that the change to two rods
was basically the same

as the one rod concept. Basically the same
as the one rod concept.
And by the licensing board's own investigation,

as reported in the American Society of Civil
Engineers' journal,

the project engineer had been asked
about the implications of the design change

on at least six separate occasions during
construction,

and assured each inquirer that the change
would not compromise the safety
of the walkways. Six times.
Nobody who asked was answered with a calculation,

because there was not one to give them.
The drawings had a hole in them as well.

Information about loads and about the connections
had appeared
on the project engineer's preliminary sketches.

It was not carried onto the final structural
drawings that went to the fabricator.

So Havens had a drawing. Sheet S four zero five
point one, sections ten and eleven.

And the tribunal that later read that sheet found
two things about it at once.
It did not communicate to the fabricator
that the fabricator was to design the connection.
And it did communicate to the fabricator

that those connections had already been designed
by the engineer.

The project engineer testified that he intended
the fabricator
to design the connections.

Havens prepared its shop drawings on the basis
that the connections shown

on the design drawings had been designed
by the structural engineer.

Each believed the other had done it. Havens sent
its shop drawings back for review.

As indicated by their stamps, they were reviewed
by the contractor,

by the structural engineer, and by the architect.
Three stamps.
The drawing did not change.

The engineering firm had a written procedure
for exactly this situation.

The Commission found, and the engineers
did not dispute,

that its own internal procedures called
for a detailed check

of all special connections. That check
did not happen.

The project engineer did not review the fourth
floor connection shown

on the shop drawings, and did not, in accord
with usual engineering practice,

assemble its components to determine what
the connection looked like in detail.

Listen to that last part again, because the film
is about to do it for him.

No review was made, and no calculations
were performed,
to determine whether the connection shown
on the shop drawings met code requirements.
Both engineers approved the shop drawings.
Under the contract, and under the statute,

review and approval of shop drawings
is an engineering function.

In October 1979, with the hotel still going up,
the atrium roof collapsed.
The investigation into that collapse established
that the cause was poor construction workmanship.

There were two accidents at the Hyatt that month,
and one of them killed a man.

The federal occupational safety agency
investigated a fatal construction accident
at the hotel in October 1979.

So twenty-one months before anybody died
in that room,
the building had already dropped something.

The owner and the architect paid the engineering
firm an additional fee to go back
and check the atrium.

The senior engineer assured the owner's
representative that he would personally look
at every connection in the hotel.

In their report to the architects, the engineers
wrote:

we then checked the suspended bridges and found
them to be satisfactory.
They had not.

The court found that they did not do a complete
check of the design of all steel

in the atrium, nor a complete check
of the suspended bridges.
What they had checked was the roof steel.
This is the most damning date in the whole file,

and it is worth being exact about why. It comes
after the change.
It comes before anybody died.

And it is a check somebody was paid to make,
and reported as made.
The atrium was inspected,

and the walkways went on hanging from a connection
nobody had ever calculated.
Then the hotel opened,

and by the following summer it had been in service
about a year.
For about a year, the building worked.

That is the part of this that is hardest to keep
hold of.

Two walkways carried people across that room,
every day, for a year,

on a connection nobody had ever calculated.
Friday, the seventeenth of July, 1981.
Kansas City is hot.

Between fifteen hundred and two thousand area
residents chose to escape the heat

at the hotel's tea dance, a weekly event with big
band music and a dance contest.

They began arriving in the middle
of the afternoon. They are not in this film.

A television crew was in that room with a camera
that evening,

and there are newspaper photographs from the hours
after it,
and none of it appears here.
It belongs to other people,

and it is a picture of a mass-casualty event
with survivors still living.

What this film has instead is the room, empty,
at three o'clock, at half past four,
and at seven.
The federal report built a timeline

of that evening out of the two Kansas City
newspapers,

and printed it in its own pages. What follows
is that timeline, in its words.

Seven o'clock. Crowd in atrium area is estimated
at fifteen hundred to two thousand.

Four minutes past. Band returns from break
and begins to play for the dance contest.
Five minutes past seven.

A non-redundant connection gives nothing away
first.

There is no second path for the load to take.
No bend, no sag, no interval.

The washer comes through the beam, and the walkway
is already falling.

The second and fourth floor walkways fell
to the atrium floor,

and the fourth floor walkway came to rest on top
of the lower one.

Most of those killed or injured were either
on the first floor level of the atrium

or on the second floor walkway. The third floor
walkway was not involved.

The two walkways together weighed a hundred
and forty-two thousand pounds.
That figure is the Missouri Court of Appeals'.

About seventy-one tons of steel and concrete,
from four storeys up.

What happened after that is in the same timeline,
and this film will not show it.

It will read it. Three minutes past the collapse,
the first call for help.

Fourteen minutes later, a call goes
out for cutting tools.
Four minutes after that, for a forklift.

By fifty-two minutes past seven there are more
than a hundred firefighters

in the building. At half past eight, a heavy crane
arrives.

At a quarter past three the following morning,
the first walkway span is lifted.

At half past four, the last survivor is removed
from the debris.

Nine hours and twenty-five minutes. The federal
report gives it eleven lines.
One hundred and fourteen people died.
At least a hundred and eighty-six were injured.

The federal report, and the engineering literature
after it,
used the same phrase for what that was.

The most devastating structural collapse ever
to take place in the United States.
This film names none of the dead.

Neither the federal report nor the court names
one,
so there is nothing here to leave out.

What there is, is a number, and a room
that had been full at five past seven.
On the twentieth of July, three days after,

Senator Thomas Eagleton's office contacted
the National Bureau of Standards

and requested that technical assistance
be provided to Kansas City.
Two days later,
the Mayor formally requested

that the Bureau independently ascertain the most
probable cause of the collapse.

Two senators and a congressman endorsed
the request.
The Bureau's people did not get a free hand.
In the early phases of the investigation,

their involvement was limited by court order
to visual and photographic observations
and measurements. Permission to weigh the spans

and to cut specimens out of them came later,
by court order,
after the parties in the litigation agreed to it.

What came out of it, in May 1982, was Building
Science Series one four three.
It is a National Bureau of Standards document,

not a National Institute of Standards
and Technology one —

the Bureau did not become the Institute
until 1988 —
and everything in this act is read out of it.
Its first conclusion is the one nobody expects.

Collapse of the walkways occurred under the action
of loads

that were substantially less than the design loads
specified
by the Kansas City Building Code. Less. Not more.
The most probable cause, it concluded,

was insufficient load capacity of the box
beam-hanger rod connections.
Two factors contributed.

The inadequacy of the original design
for the connection,
which was identical for all three walkways.

And the change in hanger rod arrangement during
construction,

which essentially doubled the load at the fourth
floor.
Now the four numbers, and they are the argument.

As drawn, the connection had to carry twenty point
three kips.

As built, the fourth floor connection had to carry
forty point seven.

At forty point seven, with a factor of safety
of one point six seven,

the code expected that connection to survive
an ultimate load
of at least sixty-eight kips.

So the Bureau built the connection again
and pulled it apart.
Across its test series,

the estimated mean ultimate capacities
of the fourth floor connections ranged

from eighteen point two kips to nineteen point
three,

with an average of eighteen point six. Sixty-eight
required.

Eighteen point six available. Then the last
number.

It is the one this case is quoted wrongly on, more
than any other.

The maximum load actually acting on a fourth floor
connection at the moment
of collapse was about twenty-one point four kips.
The Bureau puts it as a percentage:

the maximum load on a fourth floor connection
at the time

of collapse was only thirty-one percent
of the ultimate capacity expected

of a connection designed under the Kansas City
Building Code.

That thirty-one percent is a load. It
is not a strength.
It says how much was on the connection,

measured against how much the code wanted
the connection to hold.

The strength ratio is a different number,
and the federal report never states it.

Eighteen point six against sixty-eight
is about twenty-seven percent,
and that figure is ours, not theirs.

Measured the other way, against the design load
rather than the ultimate capacity,

the load on the night was fifty-three percent
of what the code required for design.

About half. Of the paper load. On a Friday
evening.

The report is just as firm about what
did not do it.

Neither the quality of workmanship
nor the materials used

in the walkway system played a significant role
in initiating the collapse.
And dancing did not do it.
Dynamic loads induced by walking or dancing

on the walkways would not have been significant
in comparison to the static loads.
That is the report's own conclusion,

and it kills the story most people have heard
about this building.

The Bureau counted the people too, as carefully
as it could.
It concluded that a total

of sixty-three people represents a credible
upper-bound combined occupancy

of the second and fourth floor walkways
at the time of collapse.
Sixty-three, at the outside,

on two bridges specified for a hundred pounds
a square foot.

The failure appears to have begun at one
connection.

Observed distortions strongly suggest that it
started at the east end

of the middle box beam in the fourth floor
walkway.
It hardly matters which one it was.

Each of the six fourth floor connections
had a high probability of failure.
Each was a candidate for initiating the collapse.

And failure of any one of them would have led
to complete collapse
of the walkway system.

Here is the hinge of the whole case, and it
is the strangest thing in the file.

Had the change never been made, the connections
would still have been illegal.

Sixty percent of code. But they would have held
that night.

The load actually on a second floor connection
at the time
of collapse was about eleven and a half kips,

against a single rod capacity of twenty
and a half.

An illegal building would have stayed up.
The change is what made it lethal.
There is an odder fact underneath that one.

Because of its greater dead load and design live
load,

the third floor walkway connection
would have had about fifty-three percent
of the expected ultimate capacity.
Had the change not been made,

the third floor walkway would have been the most
critical of the three.
The walkway that survived was the weakest one.

Redrawing the fourth floor detail is what moved
the failure to the fourth floor.
And the third walkway was never safe either.
It had, the Commission found,

a high probability of failure during the life
of the building.
With the change, the report says,

the ultimate capacity of the walkways
was so significantly reduced that from the day

of construction they had only minimal capacity
to resist their own weight,

and virtually no capacity to resist additional
loads imposed by people.

From the day of construction. Not from the day
of the dance.
No one was ever charged with a crime.
In December 1983,

the county prosecutor and the United States
Attorney announced

that they had found insufficient evidence
to convict anyone involved

in the Hyatt construction with criminal
negligence,
and that no criminal charges would be filed.
By that date,

insurance companies had paid
out over seventy-eight million dollars

to settle civil lawsuits filed by many
of the victims and their families,

and no one had yet taken responsibility
for the collapse.
What happened instead came from a licensing board.

In February 1984, the Missouri Board
for Architects,

Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors filed
a complaint seeking a determination

that the certificates of registration of Daniel
Duncan and Jack Gillum,

and the certificate of authority of their firm,
were subject to discipline.

It went to the state's Administrative Hearing
Commission,

and the Commission conducted twenty-seven days
of hearing.

Its decision runs four hundred and forty-two
pages.
Ninety-eight of findings of fact,

three hundred and twenty-two of conclusions
of law,

a hundred and eighty numbered findings —
of which the engineers challenged five.
It was filed on the fifteenth of November, 1985.

The project engineer was found guilty of gross
negligence in the preparation
and completion of a structural drawing,

and in failing to review shop drawings
of the Hyatt project.

He was further found guilty of misconduct
in misrepresenting

to the architects the safety of a connection
when he was ignorant of that safety,

due to a failure to perform the engineering tests
and calculations
that would have determined it.

The senior engineer was found vicariously liable
and responsible for the acts
and omissions of the project engineer —

a liability he assumed by affixing
his professional engineering seal
to the structural drawings.

He was further found grossly negligent in failing
to review,
or to assure that somebody had reviewed,
that drawing before affixing his seal to it.

And he was found to have engaged in unprofessional
conduct,

in failing and refusing to take responsibility
for the entire engineering project.

His answer is in the record, in a footnote,
under cross-examination.
Asked whether his seal made him responsible

for shop drawings prepared under another
engineer's direction, he answered:

because the shop drawings that were prepared
under the direction

of another engineer have to be the responsibility
of the other engineer.

They were not prepared under my direction
and therefore I cannot accept
that responsibility. In essence, the court wrote,

he placed the responsibility for the improper
design of the connections
on the fabricator,

and took the position that the structural engineer
was entitled to rely

on the fabricator's expertise. The answer
to that is a statute.
By section three two seven point four one one,

the owner of the seal is responsible for the whole
engineering project

when he places his seal on any plans — unless he
expressly disclaims responsibility,
and specifies the documents he disclaims.

The responsibility for the structural integrity
and safety

of the walkway connections was the project
engineer's,
and that responsibility was non-delegable.

Reliance upon others to perform that duty,
the court held,
serves as no justification for indifference to it.

The administrative law judge put the same idea
in one line:
while the engineer may properly delegate the work

of performing engineering design functions, he
cannot delegate the responsibility.

Gross negligence had never been defined
in a Missouri licensing case
before this one.

The Commission defined it as an act or course
of conduct

which demonstrates a conscious indifference
to a professional duty.
The structural engineer's duty, the court wrote,
is to determine that the plans he designs
or approves will provide structural safety,

because if they do not a strong probability
of harm exists.

Indifference to the duty is indifference
to the harm.

And then the finding that separates
this from a disaster story.
The discipline was not for the deaths.
That breach occurred, the court held,

at the latest when their design was incorporated
into the building
with their approval —
and they were subject

to discipline whether or not any collapse
subsequently occurred.
It was not any single act, either.

The Commission's own footnote says it is only
after a complete analysis

of their overall performance within the system
that any judgment
of their conduct can be made.
The court agreed:

it is the combination of a series of acts
and omissions
which created the structurally unsound walkways.
And in a footnote of its own,

the court concedes the thing that makes this worth
thirty minutes.

The original inadequacies of the structural
drawings might not have been critical

if a meaningful review of the shop drawings
had occurred.
Every person in that chain did something ordinary.
A drawing left a detail to the fabricator.
A fabricator solved a fabricating problem.

An engineer answered a question the way engineers
answer questions.
Three parties stamped a drawing.

Nothing in the record says that any of them wanted
a building to fall.
The Board revoked all three certificates.

It carried out the punishment on the twenty-second
of January, 1986,
four and a half years after the walkway collapse,

and the two Hyatt engineers became the first
to lose their licenses
for gross negligence. They appealed.
On the twenty-sixth of January, 1988,

the Missouri Court of Appeals reversed one finding
—

a charge of misconduct arising from the atrium
design review,
which had not been pleaded in the complaint —

and in all other respects affirmed the order
of the Commission

and the discipline imposed by the Board.
The revocations stood.
The profession had its own turn.

The American Society of Civil Engineers
had rewritten its code of ethics in 1976,

and its first fundamental canon read: engineers
shall hold paramount the safety,

health and welfare of the public
in the performance of their professional duties.

The Hyatt was the first real test
of that sentence.

The society's conduct committee heard the matter
in confidence in the summer
of 1986, and two of its members stood aside —
the chair of the Missouri licensing board,
and the man who had led the federal investigation.
The committee members concluded unanimously

that the senior engineer should be expelled,
with no privilege ever to rejoin.

The board of direction did not do that. It voted
to suspend him for three years.
He then relinquished his membership altogether.

The project engineer faced no ethics committee
at all.

He had never been a member of any national
society. Twenty point three, as drawn.

Forty point seven, as built. Sixty-eight,
as the code required.

Eighteen point six, as the steel could actually
give.

Nothing on that walkway got weaker. One beam
was asked to carry two.
The three walkways were removed.

In their place stands a single span, supported
not by delicate, graceful rods,
but standing on stout, sturdy columns.
That description was written in the year 2000,
and this film has not been back to check it.

The record this film is built on ends with a court
of appeals in January 1988.

What either engineer has done since, where they
are,

or what they think about it now is not in any
document we retrieved,
and this film does not guess.

One hundred and fourteen people went to a tea
dance and did not come home.

The connection that failed was a rod, a washer,
a nut, and a hole through a beam.

A state board found that responsibility for it
could not be handed to anybody else.
